analysis.one_liner: Cuts power plant sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, carbon dioxide, and mercury emissions by up to 90% by 2008.
analysis.headline: The Senate environment committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar on November 19, 2002, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to force power plants to sharply cut four pollutants: sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide (the causes of acid rain and smog), mercury (a poison that contaminates fish), and carbon dioxide (the main greenhouse gas). It capped national emissions at set tonnage levels starting in 2008, created a tradeable emission-allowance system, required plants older than 30 years to finally meet modern pollution standards, and handed much of the value of the emission allowances to households, workers who lost jobs, and clean-energy projects. The bill was reported out of committee but never came to the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants, including children exposed to mercury and smog; residents of acid-rain-damaged regions like the Adirondacks and Chesapeake Bay; households, who would have received a share of the value of emission allowances; and workers and communities that would have received transition assistance from allowance sales.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind residents, households, and coal-region workers

how_it_helps.text: Caps national power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide at 2.25 million tons, nitrogen oxides at 1.51 million tons, carbon dioxide at 2.05 billion tons, and mercury at just 5 tons per year starting in 2008 [S3][S4].

Requires electricity generating facilities in operation 30 years or more to meet modern new-source pollution standards, closing a loophole that let grandfathered old coal plants pollute far more than new ones [S2][S4].
Allocates remaining emission allowances (after industry allocations) to households served by electricity, with trustees to sell them at fair market value and distribute the proceeds [S3][S4].

Provides transition assistance funded by allowance sales to dislocated workers and to communities hit disproportionately by the emission reductions, plus allocations to renewable generators, efficiency projects, and cleaner energy sources [S3][S4].

Prohibits trading of mercury allowances and requires that captured mercury not be re-released into the environment, and directs the EPA to set standards for other hazardous air pollutants from coal plants [S3][S4].
Requires ambient air monitoring around large coal plants within a 30-mile radius, with results made available to the public [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired power plants and other fossil-fuel generators, who would face major compliance costs and the loss of the free-pollution status quo; coal mines supplying those plants; and electricity ratepayers to the extent compliance costs were passed through in power prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would have been concentrated on coal-dependent utilities and coal-producing regions, and the bill's own transition-assistance program for dislocated workers and hard-hit communities acknowledges that job losses and local economic damage were expected [S3][S4].

The cap-and-trade allowance system lets some plants buy allowances instead of cutting their own pollution, which can concentrate pollution around specific facilities; the bill responds with local-impact limits and trading studies, but critics argued trading weakens health protections near individual plants [S3][S4].
Electricity prices for households and businesses, particularly in coal-reliant states, would likely have risen as plants installed controls or switched fuels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits were large and broad: power plants were the source of roughly 40% of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions as well as most mercury and acid-rain pollution, and the bill capped all four [S4]. The costs were real but narrower: higher electricity prices and concentrated losses in coal-mining and coal-plant communities, which the bill tried to soften with allowance-funded transition aid and household allocations [S3][S4]. An honest accounting favors the bill on public health and climate grounds, while acknowledging it would have imposed genuine, geographically concentrated pain that the transition provisions only partly offset.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved the bill with an amended substitute and placed it on the Senate calendar in November 2002, but the Congress ended two months later without the Senate ever taking it up.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Jeffords introduced the bill on March 15, 2001, and it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee [S1][S6].
The committee's Clean Air subcommittee held five rounds of hearings between July 2001 and June 2002 [S6].
On June 27, 2002, the full committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S6].

On November 19, 2002, the committee reported the bill with a written report and minority views filed by the committee's Republicans, and the bill was placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders [S6][S3].
The bill sat on the Senate calendar without ever receiving a floor vote, and the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, killing the bill [S6][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning electric utilities and coal producers came out ahead: they avoided the first-ever federal cap on power plant carbon dioxide emissions and deep cuts in sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, and mercury, and the nation's oldest, dirtiest plants kept operating under pre-existing rules.

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, held subcommittee hearings, and managed it through the committee, which reported it favorably with a substitute amendment in November 2002.

for.name: 19 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Lieberman, Kerry, Clinton, Biden, Feinstein, and Boxer.

for.name: 3 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Collins, Snowe, and Chafee).

against.name: Republican members of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views when the committee reported the bill on November 19, 2002.

against.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor after it was placed on the calendar; it died there at the end of the Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: The administration opposed mandatory power plant carbon dioxide cuts and put forward its competing 'Clear Skies' plan covering only three pollutants, backing the weaker alternative during the same period.

against.name: Coal-burning electric utilities and coal producers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against four-pollutant power plant emission caps, particularly the carbon dioxide limit, during the committee's consideration.

sides.party_line_note: Support was mostly Democratic: 19 of 49 Senate Democrats cosponsored versus 3 of 49 Republicans, and the committee report carried minority views filed by Republicans; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call exists.

industries.note: The bill would have capped their sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, carbon dioxide, and mercury emissions at sharply lower levels by 2008 and required 30-year-old plants to meet modern standards, forcing expensive retrofits or fuel switches. Its defeat preserved the old plants' ability to operate under pre-1990 pollution rules.

Deep cuts in pollutants, including the first federal cap on power plant carbon dioxide, would have reduced demand for coal used in electricity generation. The bill included allowance-funded transition assistance aimed partly at the coal-dependent communities that would be hurt.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency industries
industries.note: The bill would have allocated up to 20% of emission allowances to renewable generators, efficient buildings and products, and clean fossil units, creating a new revenue stream that grows as pollution limits tighten.

Tightening coal plant limits would push some generation toward natural gas, but the bill also required demand-side and supply-side policies to reduce the rate of growth of gas consumption, hedging against price increases for consumers.
Higher electricity prices would raise their costs, but the bill allocated a declining share of allowances to producers of electricity-intensive products as transition assistance.
